items.title: The Windrush passengers were British subjects, not foreign immigrants
items.claim: On 22 June 1948 the HMT Empire Windrush docked at Tilbury with 492 passengers from the Caribbean. Their legal status?

options.text: They required visas and work permits
They were British subjects with full right of entry — the British Nationality Act 1948 confirmed Commonwealth citizens' status, passed weeks after Windrush
They were refugees with temporary leave
They were on military service tickets only

items.reveal:
The British Nationality Act 1948 (royal assent 30 July 1948) defined 'Citizens of the United Kingdom and Colonies' alongside Commonwealth citizenship. Caribbean people were British subjects; the journey required no permit.

The 1971 Immigration Act removed automatic right of abode for most Commonwealth citizens. People who had arrived as children before 1973 should have had right to remain, but the Home Office destroyed landing card records in 2010 — leading to the Windrush scandal of 2018, when long-resident citizens were detained, deported or denied healthcare.

The Windrush brought around 1,000 passengers total, including Jamaicans returning from RAF service.
items.why: Right of abode in Britain has been redefined repeatedly. The 1948-1973 period when Commonwealth citizens had unrestricted entry is bracketed by very different regimes — and the 2018 scandal shows what happens when administrative memory fails.

items.title: The Dissolution of the Monasteries was a wealth transfer
items.claim: Henry VIII dissolved the monasteries (1536-1541). How much was at stake financially?

options.text: A symbolic amount; most monasteries were poor
The monasteries owned around a quarter of the cultivated land in England; their dissolution transferred wealth equivalent to several times the crown's annual income
The proceeds were used to found grammar schools across the country
Only the buildings were seized; lands remained in religious hands

items.reveal:
Thomas Cromwell's Valor Ecclesiasticus (1535) surveyed monastic incomes — around £160,000 a year, against royal ordinary revenue of about £100,000. The Court of Augmentations was created to handle the proceeds.

Much of the land was sold below market to gentry buyers, creating a new class with a stake in keeping the Reformation. Cathedrals like Glastonbury were destroyed; libraries were dispersed (John Leland's lament). The wealth was largely spent on war with France within a decade.
items.why: The break with Rome was about Anne Boleyn and the king's conscience — but it was also the biggest fiscal opportunity an English king had had since the Conquest. Mixed motives, both real.

items.title: British smallpox vaccination became compulsory in 1853
items.claim: When did vaccination become compulsory in the UK?

options.text: The Vaccination Act 1853 made infant smallpox vaccination compulsory in England and Wales; the 1867 Act introduced fines for non-compliance; the 1898 Act allowed a 'conscientious objection' exemption after mass protest
It was made compulsory only in 1948

items.reveal:
Edward Jenner published his cowpox technique in 1798. The 1853 Vaccination Act required parents to vaccinate infants within three months of birth, or face fines. The 1867 Act added imprisonment for repeated refusal.

The Leicester Anti-Vaccination League (founded 1869) led mass protest; in 1885, around 100,000 marched in Leicester against the Act. The 'Leicester method' substituted isolation and sanitation for compulsory vaccination — and Leicester's smallpox mortality remained low.

The 1898 Act introduced 'conscientious objection' as a legal category. Smallpox was declared eradicated globally by WHO on 8 May 1980 — the only human disease ever eradicated.
items.why: Public health enforcement has always provoked opposition. The 19th-century vaccination debate created the legal category of 'conscientious objection' — a concept later used for military service and other state requirements.
